title: The smith and the silver (239–243)
hookLine: as a smith removes impurities from silver, little by little; ignorance the greatest taint

lines: A FAINT GLEAM AT THE EDGE.
THE SILVER WAS THERE ALL ALONG.
cards: Take out an old silver spoon, the kind that sat in a drawer for years. It's gone dark, almost black in places. Rub it with a soft cloth and a little polish, and at first nothing happens.
Then a faint gleam appears at the edge of the bowl. Rub more, and a little more of it comes back. You can't polish the whole spoon in one stroke.
But stroke by stroke, the silver was there all along. Chapter eighteen of the Dhammapada puts a silversmith right in the middle of its teaching.

teach.h: THE SMITH BLOWS OFF THE DROSS.
teach.b: Verse two thirty-nine, in Max Müller's translation: "Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time."
Picture an ancient smith at the furnace, melting silver and blowing the dross off the top, not all of it in one breath. The chapter's name is Malavagga, and mala means a stain, a taint, the dross.
The old commentary tells of a brahmin who noticed monks' robes getting wet from dew as they walked through long grass, so he cleared the grass. Later he saw them getting dusty, so he spread sand.
Then he built a shelter against the sun and rain.

teach.h: A BRAHMIN, ONE SMALL THING AT A TIME.
teach.b: One small thing at a time, never a grand plan, and the Buddha praised him with this verse. Then the chapter lists taints, the way a household list would.
Verse two forty-one: "The taint of prayers is non-repetition; the taint of houses, non-repair". A chant you stop reciting fades from memory. A house you stop mending falls apart.
Neglect is its own kind of stain.
Then the heaviest line, verse two forty-three: "But there is a taint worse than all taints,--ignorance is the greatest taint." Ignorance, avijjā, isn't about not knowing facts.

It's not seeing how things really are: that they change, that craving hurts. The verse calls it worse than all the rest, and ends by telling the monks to throw it off. Which is why the polishing never stops.

how: Buddhist practice is often described as gradual purification, and teachers use the smith and the silver to encourage steady daily effort rather than dramatic change.

o: a sin that can never be washed away
a stain or taint, like dross on silver

games.q: match each taint to what it is.

s: the smith clears the silver all at once
"one by one, little by little, and from time to time."
verse 243 names ignorance as the greatest taint
in the commentary, the brahmin began with a grand plan
he cleared some grass, then spread sand, then built a shelter, one small thing at a time.

games.q: you're the brahmin who sees monks' robes soaked with dew from the long grass. what do you do first?
o: tell them to walk another way.
games.why: he cleared the grass, then spread sand, then built a shelter: one small thing at a time, and the Buddha praised him.

practice: If you can, pick up something small that needs care, a spoon, your glasses, a mug with a stain, or picture one, and slowly wipe it, just a little, noticing the small change.

Then close your eyes and do the same with the mind: with each out-breath, let one small speck of irritation or worry blow off the top, like dross from silver. Not all of it; one by one, little by little.

wordCard.voice: Mala. A stain, a taint, the dross: verse two thirty-nine says as a smith blows the impurities off silver, one by one, little by little, the wise clear their own.

orig.note: Pali: stain, taint, impurity — chapter eighteen is the Malavagga; avijjā paramaṃ malaṃ, ignorance is the greatest taint.

carryVoice: Your line: little by little. One by one, and from time to time. On we go.
